title: Camp 4 close: back to Galilee
hook: the young man said: he's going ahead of you to Galilee, back where it all began (Mark 16:7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the longer ending of Mark, and your line was go into all the world. Did you turn one fear into a small errand? Day two hundred thirty-one. The end of the week, and the close of camp four.

Have you ever gone back to your hometown after something big happened? The streets are the same. The diner is the same. But you're not. You notice things you walked past a hundred times. At the empty tomb, the young man in white gave the women a message for the disciples. In the King James Bible: "he goeth before you into Galilee: there shall ye see him, as he said unto you." Not to Rome. Not to the temple. Back to Galilee. Back to the lake, the boats, the nets, the little towns where it all began.
screen: `BACK TO YOUR HOMETOWN.` → `HE GOETH BEFORE YOU INTO GALILEE.` → `WHERE IT ALL BEGAN.`

segments.voice: For seventy-five days, this camp has read one book, the Gospel of Mark, in order, a few verses at a time. Let's walk back through it. It began with a single line: the beginning of the good news. Then the heavens torn open, and fishermen told to leave the nets. Friends dug through a roof. A leper heard I am willing. A sower threw seed everywhere, and Jesus slept on a cushion in a storm. A little girl heard talitha koum, get up. Five thousand were fed, and a woman told she was a dog answered back, and her daughter was healed. At Caesarea Philippi came the question at the center of the book: who do you say I am? Then the road to Jerusalem: take up your cross; a blind man named Bartimaeus asked to see; a widow gave all she had. And in these last days of the camp: perfume poured out, bread broken, abba in the garden, Peter weeping by the fire, a crown of thorns, the women who stayed, and an empty tomb. Now here's why Galilee matters. Mark's ending sends the disciples back to the beginning. Some readers think Mark wants his readers, too, to go back to chapter one and read it again, knowing how it ends. The disciples misunderstood again and again the first time through. Read again, the same stories look different. The very first verse, in the King James Bible, says: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." The beginning. As if the whole book is only the start. Tomorrow a new camp begins: camp five, the depths, and it opens with Jesus sitting down on a mountain to teach.
screen: `SEVENTY-FIVE DAYS OF MARK.` · `FROM THE NETS TO THE EMPTY TOMB.` · `BACK TO GALILEE, BACK TO CHAPTER ONE.` · `CAMP FIVE: THE DEPTHS.` · then, large: `THE BEGINNING OF THE GOSPEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reread Mark 1:1. If you can, open a Bible to the first verse of Mark and read it slowly, the way you'd read it now, after everything. The beginning of the gospel. Notice which word lands differently this time. If you can't open it, say the words quietly to yourself. Then think back over this camp. Which one story from Mark stays with you most? Let it come up on its own. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. The bell holds the time.
Camp four close. Seventy-five days reading Mark in order, from the beginning of the good news to an empty tomb, and a message: back to Galilee.
Your line: start again, knowing more. Today, go back to something familiar: a street, a song, a person. Notice what you see now that you didn't see before. Day two hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Churches that follow a lectionary read through one Gospel across a year of Sundays; in the three-year cycle shared by Catholics and a number of Protestant churches, Mark is the Gospel of the second year.

notes: Camp close: names camp four's stories (days 157–231) and points at camp five.
'Son of God' in Mark 1:1 is missing from a few early manuscripts (e.g. Sinaiticus first hand); the KJV includes it. Keeper may want a note.
Mark is read in Year B of the Revised Common Lectionary and the Catholic Lectionary; confirm howItsDone phrasing.
The circular reading (the ending sending readers back to 1:1) is one interpretation, phrased as 'many readers think'.
